messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Robert was seven years old when his uncle came home smelling of cheap whiskey, the same smell that now stopped him mid-stride outside a liquor store. His uncle had been the one person his mother trusted to watch him while she worked nights, and for three years that trust was repaid with a palm that left bruises and a belt that left welts. No one ever asked about the marks. No one ever came. The man still lived two towns over, unpunished, unaccountable — a fact that had calcified into a bitter certainty: the people responsible had faced no consequences, and that meant the world was not a place where safety was enforced.

The smell of alcohol could still hijack his nervous system in an instant. It would waft from a passerby’s breath or from a bar as he walked past, and suddenly he was not a seventy-one-year-old insurance agent on a sidewalk — he was a child again, waiting for the footsteps. The memory came as a fragment, just a flash of a brown leather belt and a hand, more vivid and real than his actual surroundings. He could smell it — the whiskey, the stale sweat — as if the air had changed. That olfactory recall did not stay contained; it triggered the old appraisal that his body was a traitor, still reacting as if danger were present when logic told him he was safe. And because the abuser had never faced justice, he had come to believe that strangers, too, were unaccountable — that any ordinary approach could turn into a violation.

Working as an insurance agent required talking to strangers daily. Every new client on the phone or at the desk felt like a potential threat. A friendly hello from a neighbor on his porch could send his heart racing. He would then check his locks twice, sometimes three times, listening for the sound of footsteps on his stairs or the click of a key in the lock — an intrusion monitoring that had become second nature. These false alarms, reacting as if he were in danger when nothing was wrong, only deepened the appraisal that his own body was an enemy, that he could not trust its signals. The stranger trigger and the threat of intrusion fed each other: a stranger’s approach activated the threat system; the threat system, in turn, made him see strangers as more dangerous than they were.

To keep the memories at bay, Robert had developed quiet rituals. Before answering the door, he would count to seven under his breath — seven for the years of abuse — and believe that if he did it perfectly, nothing bad would happen that day. He kept his mind occupied constantly, filling his hours with paperwork, radio, crossword puzzles, anything to avoid the sudden fragments that could surface without warning. He stopped watching television dramas or reading news stories that involved child abuse; he knew the triggers were too close. But these strategies also reinforced the sense that something required constant vigilance. The mental rituals implied that danger was always latent, that without them he would be vulnerable, and that his own mind could not be trusted to simply let the past lie. Each ritual confirmed the betrayal narrative: no one had protected him then, so he had to protect himself now, even from his own thoughts.

The memories themselves were sporadic but punishing. A fragment would appear — the feel of a hand on his collar, the sound of a belt buckle — and vanish just as quickly, leaving him disoriented. Those fragments often brought the smell with them, and the smell was the most direct link to the original threat. Because the memories felt more real than his ordinary life, they overrode his present-moment safety cues, triggering the same defensive reactions he had as a child. He would freeze, scan the room, listen for footsteps. The memory fed the threat; the threat, in turn, made the memory more intrusive — a loop that tightened with each pass.

Now, at seventy-one, Robert had begun to notice that his avoidance was costing him. A colleague had retired, and he was forced to take on more client-facing work. He dreaded each call. He had considered early retirement but worried that he could not afford it and that the empty hours would leave him alone with the fragments. His sleep had grown restless; he often woke at 2 a.m., sure he had heard someone in the apartment. Last week a siren from an ambulance passing his building sent him to the floor without thinking. That was the moment he finally called the clinic. He was tired of counting, tired of checking locks, tired of being afraid of a man who was old and might not even be alive. What frightened him most was the possibility that the fear would never stop — that his body would always be the enemy, and that the world he had to live in would always feel as dangerous as the one he had survived.
